Behest

bih-HEST -- stress on the second syllable, HEST. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Behest is an urgent request, order, or command, especially from someone in authority.

At the mayor's behest, the city council moved its meeting to the larger auditorium so more residents could attend.

Worked Example

The director makes a single phone call, and by the next morning the entire film crew has assembled on set two weeks ahead of schedule.

The crew gathered at the director's behest -- an urgent order from someone with the authority to make it happen. Behest almost always appears in the fixed phrase 'at someone's behest,' marking a command weighty enough to set other people in motion.

How Behest Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

command

command: an authoritative order that expects obedience

bidding

bidding: an order or request; what someone directs you to do

directive

directive: an official instruction issued by an authority

Antonyms

suggestion

suggestion: an idea offered for consideration, not an order

entreaty

entreaty: a humble, earnest plea from a position of weakness

How Strong Is It? — bidding → behest → command

bidding vs. behest

bidding vs. behest: Bidding is softer and more old-fashioned than behest -- doing someone's bidding may follow a mild request, while a behest carries urgency and the full weight of the requester's authority.

command vs. behest

command vs. behest: Command is even more forceful than behest: a behest is an urgent request that leans on authority and respect, while a command is a direct order that expects obedience with no discussion at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — be-

prefix — be-: thoroughly, about (Old English)

root — hest/hat-

root — hest/hat-: to command, to promise (Old English hatan)

Put it together

Put it together: Behest comes from Old English behaes, 'a vow or promise,' built on hatan, 'to command or promise.' Over the centuries the promise side faded and the command side won out: a behest today is an authoritative order -- something promised into action by the person with the power to demand it.

Use the root in a new word: behold

Use the root in a new word: behold: The hikers reached the ridge at dawn to behold the entire valley glowing below them.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Behest lives almost entirely inside one fixed phrase: 'at someone's behest' -- at the king's behest, at her behest, at the committee's behest. If you find yourself writing behest without 'at' and a possessive in front of it, rework the sentence; the collocation is the word.
